news.full_article_text: IIT Kharagpur becomes first IIT to offer MD programmes approved by national medical body IIT Kharagpur become the first IIT to offer postgraduate medical courses recognised by NMC, introducing 12 MD seats across six specialisations. Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur in West Bengal has become the first IIT in India to introduce postgraduate medical degree programmes recognised by the National Medical Commission (NMC), offering 12 MD seats across six specialisations for the 2026-27 academic session, the institute announced on Thursday. “The Institute undertook the prescribed regulatory process with the NMC, including submission of applications, documentation of academic and clinical facilities, and fulfilment of the applicable requirements in March 2026. The process culminated in permission for the six MD programmes for the academic session 2026–27,” director of IIT Kharagpur Suman Chakraborty said. The programmes will be offered at the institute’s Dr B C Roy Multi-Speciality Medical Research Centre, with admissions through the second round of NEET-PG 2026 counselling from November 10 to 23, according to the announcement. Fees of the PG medical course and stipends paid to students will be on the lines of AIIMS. “The postgraduate medical programmes are supported by the in-house expanding clinical infrastructure of Dr. Shyama Prasad Mookerji Superspeciality Hospital - new Hospital of IIT Kharagpur, together with the South Eastern Railway Hospital, Kharagpur, under the established institutional partnership. This arrangement provides the clinical training ecosystem for the approved postgraduate programmes, in accordance with the applicable NMC requirements,” Chakraborty said. The six specialisations are general medicine, radiology, physiology, pathology, community medicine and biochemistry, with two seats in each discipline. The programmes will be available for eligible candidates through the Medical Counselling Committee’s (MCC) online counselling process. MCC is the government body responsible for conducting online counselling to allot medical and dental seats based on NEET scores. The move marks the entry of an IIT into postgraduate medical education and is aimed at bringing clinical medicine closer to engineering, artificial intelligence (AI), biomedical sciences and translational research. IIT Kharagpur said in a statement that the programmes would provide opportunities for medical students to engage with research across areas such as AI-assisted clinical decision-making, advanced medical imaging, computational pathology, biomedical devices, molecular diagnostics, precision medicine and population health. The institute added that its existing strengths in microfluidics, bioengineering, healthcare diagnostics, AI, computational sciences and translational medical technologies would provide a foundation for the interdisciplinary approach. Chakraborty said the institute’s objective was not limited to training specialist doctors but also included developing medical professionals capable of addressing healthcare challenges through research and technology. “India’s first IIT is now taking a historic step towards shaping the future of medical education. Our vision is not simply to train specialist doctors, but to create an ecosystem where clinical excellence meets engineering ingenuity, artificial intelligence and translational research,” he said. “We want our medical graduates to be not only outstanding clinicians, but also innovators capable of addressing some of humanity’s most pressing healthcare challenges,” Chakraborty added. He said the first batch would be pioneers of a new academic journey, with the institute aiming to nurture doctors who can combine clinical understanding with scientific discovery and technological innovation. Established in 1951, IIT Kharagpur was the first institute in the IIT system. Its entry into postgraduate medical education comes in its 75th year and is part of its broader ambition to expand the role of technological institutions in addressing healthcare challenges. The institute also said that it has identified research-driven learning and international academic exposure as elements of the proposed academic environment. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Sanjay Maurya Sanjay Maurya is a Principal Correspondent with Hindustan Times, where he covers education, with a focus on school and higher education, competitive examinations, education policy and governance. news.headline: Was Delhi pollution data during Diwali misleading?
news.story_lead: - Published 12 November 2026, 09:01 GMT BBC Verify has found significant discrepancies between two Indian government datasets showing Delhi's air pollution during Diwali, indicating official figures may not have captured the full extent of the problem. As fireworks lit up Delhi's skies on 8 November to mark one of India's biggest festivals, some monitoring stations recorded very high levels of PM2.5, a fine particulate matter which can damage people's lungs and cause other serious health problems. But every hourly PM2.5 reading above 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre was excluded from the widely cited air quality index (AQI) published by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), even though these higher readings were present in the data from the Delhi Pollution Control Commission (DPCC).
news.full_article_text: - Published 12 November 2026, 09:01 GMT BBC Verify has found significant discrepancies between two Indian government datasets showing Delhi's air pollution during Diwali, indicating official figures may not have captured the full extent of the problem. As fireworks lit up Delhi's skies on 8 November to mark one of India's biggest festivals, some monitoring stations recorded very high levels of PM2.5, a fine particulate matter which can damage people's lungs and cause other serious health problems. But every hourly PM2.5 reading above 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre was excluded from the widely cited air quality index (AQI) published by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), even though these higher readings were present in the data from the Delhi Pollution Control Commission (DPCC). Delhi is one of the most polluted cities in the world and often has dangerously poor air quality , so it is vital people living in India's capital can trust the official data. Firecrackers are not the only cause of pollution, which is also attributed to a mix of reasons including vehicle emissions, construction dust, farm fires and atmospheric factors. But they can worsen air quality, especially in winter. Government critics and opposition parties have accused the government of deliberately under-reporting the pollution data. The CPCB rejected this in a statement, which said the body was "committed to transparent, scientific and reliable reporting". The CPCB, whose figures are generally cited by Indian media, said readings above 1,000 micrograms are treated as "outside" the range for detection its equipment has been calibrated for and are excluded from calculations. "During extreme episodes which are occasional like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of relevant pollutant for concerned station," the statement added. Dr Manoj Kumar, a researcher at Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), told BBC Verify that excluding high readings risks misrepresenting actual pollution levels and could cause people to lose trust in official figures. Our analysis found that, across the same 30 stations over 24 hours covering Diwali night, available CPCB readings averaged 240 micrograms per cubic metre - less than half the average of 551 in DPCC's data. What does the pollution data show? On the night of Diwali from Sunday into Monday, Delhi's already high pollution levels rose sharply as the celebrations peaked. Three different pollution monitoring stations recorded PM2.5 hourly concentrations above 3,000 micrograms, DPCC data examined by BBC Verify shows. Dr Kumar said that even a short-term exposure to extreme levels of particulate matter can have adverse health impacts. The World Health Organization's air quality guidelines state that annual average concentrations should not exceed five micrograms per cubic metre. Between 21:00 local time (15:30 GMT) on 8 November and 07:00 on 9 November, during the peak of Diwali celebrations, 217 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 16 stations reported complete data during this period, while 43 had at least one missing observation. None of the 116 readings above 1,000 micrograms from the 30 DPCC-managed stations appeared in the CPCB's published records they feed data into. This matters because stations need at least 16 hours of valid PM2.5 measurements to calculate a daily average, according to CPCB's methodology. So a station with too many missing or invalid readings will not contribute to official pollution calculations. One example of a station with several hours of missing data was at RK Puram in south Delhi, where pollution peaked at nearly 2,500 micrograms. Using hourly PM2.5 readings from this station, BBC Verify calculated an average concentration of about 945 micrograms over the 24-hour period after 17:00 on 8 November. But similar averages of CPCB's published data for 14 of those 24 hours produced a much lower figure of 299 micrograms. The missing 10 hours also meant this data was not included in daily average calculations. The missing data across the city means that, despite a sharp overnight rise in pollution at some monitoring stations, CPCB reported Delhi's AQI at 344 at 16:00 on 9 November, down from 376 at the same time the day before. Dr Sierra Clark, an environmental epidemiologist from City St George's, University in London, warned classifying high pollution readings as missing could leave out days which "contribute the most to short-term health events, such as asthma attacks and heart attacks". She told BBC Verify "for transparency", Delhi's pollution reporting could show two scenarios including and excluding extreme pollution episodes. "The latter would give a sense of typical pollution levels that are more representative of people's day-to-day experience. But it is also important to show the impact of those few days and what they contribute," Dr Clark added. Pollution in Delhi is not limited to PM2.5 and satellite imagery shows a thick haze over the city on 8 and 9 November. Satellite measurements of other pollutants like nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO) and fire activity in the atmosphere, rather than at ground level, showed increases on 8 November. But their overall average for Diwali week was not very high compared with 2024 and 2025. Graphics by Jess Carr and Tom Shiel. What do you want BBC Verify to investigate? hindi_translation.full_article_text: - Published 12 November 2026, 09:01 GMT BBC Verify has found significant discrepancies between two Indian government datasets showing Delhi's air pollution during Diwali, indicating official figures may not have captured the full extent of the problem. As fireworks lit up Delhi's skies on 8 November to mark one of India's biggest festivals, some monitoring stations recorded very high levels of PM2.5, a fine particulate matter which can damage people's lungs and cause other serious health problems. But every hourly PM2.5 reading above 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre was excluded from the widely cited air quality index (AQI) published by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), even though these higher readings were present in the data from the Delhi Pollution Control Commission (DPCC). Delhi is one of the most polluted cities in the world and often has dangerously poor air quality , so it is vital people living in India's capital can trust the official data. Firecrackers are not the only cause of pollution, which is also attributed to a mix of reasons including vehicle emissions, construction dust, farm fires and atmospheric factors. But they can worsen air quality, especially in winter. Government critics and opposition parties have accused the government of deliberately under-reporting the pollution data. The CPCB rejected this in a statement, which said the body was "committed to transparent, scientific and reliable reporting". The CPCB, whose figures are generally cited by Indian media, said readings above 1,000 micrograms are treated as "outside" the range for detection its equipment has been calibrated for and are excluded from calculations. "During extreme episodes which are occasional like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of relevant pollutant for concerned station," the statement added. Dr Manoj Kumar, a researcher at Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), told BBC Verify that excluding high readings risks misrepresenting actual pollution levels and could cause people to lose trust in official figures. Our analysis found that, across the same 30 stations over 24 hours covering Diwali night, available CPCB readings averaged 240 micrograms per cubic metre - less than half the average of 551 in DPCC's data. What does the pollution data show? On the night of Diwali from Sunday into Monday, Delhi's already high pollution levels rose sharply as the celebrations peaked. Three different pollution monitoring stations recorded PM2.5 hourly concentrations above 3,000 micrograms, DPCC data examined by BBC Verify shows. Dr Kumar said that even a short-term exposure to extreme levels of particulate matter can have adverse health impacts. The World Health Organization's air quality guidelines state that annual average concentrations should not exceed five micrograms per cubic metre. Between 21:00 local time (15:30 GMT) on 8 November and 07:00 on 9 November, during the peak of Diwali celebrations, 217 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 16 stations reported complete data during this period, while 43 had at least one missing observation. None of the 116 readings above 1,000 micrograms from the 30 DPCC-managed stations appeared in the CPCB's published records they feed data into. This matters because stations need at least 16 hours of valid PM2.5 measurements to calculate a daily average, according to CPCB's methodology. So a station with too many missing or invalid readings will not contribute to official pollution calculations. One example of a station with several hours of missing data was at RK Puram in south Delhi, where pollution peaked at nearly 2,500 micrograms. Using hourly PM2.5 readings from this station, BBC Verify calculated an average concentration of about 945 micrograms over the 24-hour period after 17:00 on 8 November. But similar averages of CPCB's published data for 14 of those 24 hours produced a much lower figure of 299 micrograms. The missing 10 hours also meant this data was not included in daily average calculations. The missing data across the city means that, despite a sharp overnight rise in pollution at some monitoring stations, CPCB reported Delhi's AQI at 344 at 16:00 on 9 November, down from 376 at the same time the day before. Dr Sierra Clark, an environmental epidemiologist from City St George's, University in London, warned classifying high pollution readings as missing could leave out days which "contribute the most to short-term health events, such as asthma attacks and heart attacks". She told BBC Verify "for transparency", Delhi's pollution reporting could show two scenarios including and excluding extreme pollution episodes. "The latter would give a sense of typical pollution levels that are more representative of people's day-to-day experience. But it is also important to show the impact of those few days and what they contribute," Dr Clark added. Pollution in Delhi is not limited to PM2.5 and satellite imagery shows a thick haze over the city on 8 and 9 November. Satellite measurements of other pollutants like nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO) and fire activity in the atmosphere, rather than at ground level, showed increases on 8 November. But their overall average for Diwali week was not very high compared with 2024 and 2025. Graphics by Jess Carr and Tom Shiel. What do you want BBC Verify to investigate? news.headline: Hegseth awards medal to war memorial guard who reprimanded him and group
news.story_lead: US Army guard reprimands group that includes US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at Arlington National Cemetery. - Published 11 November 2026 US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a medal to the guard who reprimanded his group at Arlington National Cemetery. A video of a Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier before the guard told them to be quiet.
news.full_article_text: US Army guard reprimands group that includes US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at Arlington National Cemetery. - Published 11 November 2026 US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a medal to the guard who reprimanded his group at Arlington National Cemetery. A video of a Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier before the guard told them to be quiet. In a statement, the Pentagon later announced that Hegseth had given Specialist Thomas Iglesias a Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier". Photos shared on the defence secretary's X account showed him presenting the medal to Iglesias. He was accompanied by others whom the Pentagon identified as members of the 3rd US Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, which is responsible for holding vigil over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots," the accompanying text on Hegseth's post reads. In the video, the army sentinel on duty later identified as Iglesias can be seen stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times." Hegseth (right) awarded the medal to Specialist Thomas Iglesias after being reprimanded by him The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct. The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell later said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum." "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured - and will always honour - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe." A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948. It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and First Lady Melania Trump bow their heads in prayer during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery. During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war. "Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back. All of us fought back," he said. "And we won," Trump said of the Iran war. "It's just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory." Trump also pointed out Hegseth during the ceremony, saying he's done a "fantastic job" as defence secretary. Trump has repeatedly defended Hegseth amid Democratic lawmakers' push to impeach him. On Tuesday, an effort to impeach the defence secretary under accusations that he waged war on Iran without congressional authorisation failed on Capitol Hill . Hegseth has called the impeachment efforts a "farce" and a "stunt". news.headline: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
news.story_lead: Bomb squads have searched many schools but no devices have been found - Published 12 November 2026, 12:39 GMT Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations. Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats to one that created chaos on Wednesday - even though no explosive devices have been found. The government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated".
news.full_article_text: Bomb squads have searched many schools but no devices have been found - Published 12 November 2026, 12:39 GMT Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations. Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats to one that created chaos on Wednesday - even though no explosive devices have been found. The government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated". Unlike a day earlier, only 77 schools were evacuated on Thursday, authorities say. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says her government will come up with "sector-specific" advice to help those facing this kind of threat. Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected. On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France. The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries. Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings. Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan". Some officials say it originated in Taiwan. A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked. - No risk to public from hoax school bomb threats, says government minister Published 1 day ago - Police treating threatening email sent to more than 300 schools as 'hoax' Published 1 day ago Many parents, though, are concerned and have been demanding clarity and action from the government. La Repubblica newspaper reports that protests have been held against a decision by the headmaster of a secondary school in Rome who did not take any action, saying she had realised the threatening message to contain typos and therefore be "fake". According to the newspaper, protesters want new national guidelines to be issued. Related topics More on this story - Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats Published 6 days ago

news.full_article_text:
### National Naturopathy Day: Significance and Health Framework

National Naturopathy Day serves as an annual national observance aimed at promoting drugless systems of healing and wellness across India. Governed under the broader mandate of the Ministry of AYUSH, the day stresses the importance of non-invasive, nature-based medical systems, preventive health interventions, and lifestyle medicine.

Key aspects associated with the observance include:
- **Focus on Research:** Encouraging clinical research and evidence-based validation of traditional naturopathic treatments and wellness therapies.
- **Preventive Healthcare:** Advocating for lifestyle modifications, natural nutrition, and stress management as primary mechanisms for disease prevention.
- **Holistic Integration:** Aligning traditional drugless therapies with modern wellness paradigms to strengthen public health outcomes.
bullet_points: National Naturopathy Day emphasizes drugless and non-invasive healthcare systems.
The day aims to raise awareness regarding nature-cure techniques and preventive medicine.
It promotes evidence-based clinical research in alternative health and wellness practices.
The policy and promotional frameworks are managed under the Ministry of AYUSH in India.

hindi_translation.story_lead: राष्ट्रीय प्राकृतिक चिकित्सा दिवस का उद्देश्य बिना दवा, निवारक और समग्र स्वास्थ्य देखभाल प्रणालियों के बारे में जागरूकता बढ़ाना है। यह दिन स्वस्थ जीवन शैली के विकल्पों को बढ़ावा देने के लिए पारंपरिक प्राकृतिक चिकित्सा पद्धतियों के साथ वैज्ञानिक अनुसंधान के एकीकरण पर जोर देता है।
hindi_translation.full_article_text:
### राष्ट्रीय प्राकृतिक चिकित्सा दिवस: महत्व और स्वास्थ्य ढांचा

राष्ट्रीय प्राकृतिक चिकित्सा दिवस पूरे भारत में प्राकृतिक और बिना दवा वाली स्वास्थ्य प्रणालियों को बढ़ावा देने के उद्देश्य से मनाया जाता है। आयुष मंत्रालय के व्यापक जनादेश के तहत संचालित, यह दिन गैर-आक्रामक, प्रकृति-आधारित चिकित्सा प्रणालियों, निवारक स्वास्थ्य हस्तक्षेपों और जीवन शैली चिकित्सा के महत्व पर बल देता है।

इस आयोजन से जुड़े प्रमुख पहलू:
- **अनुसंधान पर ध्यान:** पारंपरिक प्राकृतिक चिकित्सा और वेलनेस थेरेपी के नैदानिक अनुसंधान और साक्ष्य-आधारित सत्यापन को प्रोत्साहित करना।
- **निवारक स्वास्थ्य देखभाल:** बीमारी की रोकथाम के प्राथमिक तरीकों के रूप में जीवन शैली में बदलाव, प्राकृतिक पोषण और तनाव प्रबंधन की वकालत करना।
- **समग्र एकीकरण:** सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य परिणामों को मजबूत करने के लिए आधुनिक वेलनेस मापदंडों के साथ पारंपरिक दवाओं का समन्वय करना।
bullet_points: राष्ट्रीय प्राकृतिक चिकित्सा दिवस बिना दवा और गैर-आक्रामक स्वास्थ्य प्रणालियों पर जोर देता है।
इस दिन का उद्देश्य प्राकृतिक चिकित्सा तकनीकों और निवारक चिकित्सा के बारे में जागरूकता बढ़ाना है।
यह वैकल्पिक स्वास्थ्य और कल्याण पद्धतियों में साक्ष्य-आधारित नैदानिक अनुसंधान को बढ़ावा देता है।
